Salvator Mundi. Salvator Mundi is a portrait of Christ holding a crystal orb, painted by Leonardo in the 1490s. Jesus gestures in blessing while gazing directly at the viewer with serene authority. The work exemplifies Leonardo's investigation of divine presence through portraiture, combining Renaissance ideals of physical beauty with spiritual majesty, though its attribution and provenance remain subjects of scholarly debate.

The painting is oil on walnut panel, measuring about 26 by 18 inches, depicting Christ as a young man of idealized features and Renaissance dignity. Christ holds a transparent crystal orb, representing the world, in his left hand while raising his right in a gesture of benediction and blessing, a pose echoing medieval iconography but infused with Renaissance grace. The painting's attribution to Leonardo has been contested: while stylistically consistent with his work, some experts question whether it is entirely autograph or partly executed by assistants.

The crystal sphere is rendered with extraordinary technical skill, demonstrating Leonardo's mastery of light refraction and transparency, a subject he investigated in his notebooks. Christ's face exhibits the soft sfumato modeling characteristic of Leonardo's portraiture, with an expression balancing humility and cosmic authority. The work exemplifies the Renaissance humanization of religious imagery: Christ appears neither stern judge nor remote deity, but a compassionate presence engaging the viewer directly. A sale at Christie's in 2017 priced a restored version at four hundred fifty point three million dollars, making it the most expensive painting ever sold at auction, though its condition and attribution remain controversial.
